TPU-Distil · October 2026

Big-model quality
at a small-model price

How we taught small models to do the job of a 552B model on SQL, finance, maths and drawing, and served each one on a single Cloud TPU chip
Jawad Amin and Fred Molina
github.com/jawadaminGOOG/tpu-distil
Welcome. This talk is about getting the quality of a big model at the price of a small one. A frontier model does specialist work well, but it needs a whole 8-GPU server. A small model is cheap, but it isn't good at the job. We used big models to teach small models on four tasks: SQL, financial questions, competition maths, and drawing pictures as SVG code. Then we served each student on TPU. Along the way we found that the recipe has to change when the student is already strong, and that when a check can only read the format, you have to look at the outputs. ~1 min.

01

The problem

Frontier models do the job well, but they are expensive and GPUs are hard to get. Small models are cheap, but they don't know the domain.
Part 1: the problem. ~6 minutes.
The problem

Big models are expensive; small ones fall short

One frontier model needs a whole GPU server
552B
parameters in the teacher, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
$36.60 / h
for one teacher replica, at the cheapest listed H200 rate
$2.70 / h
for one TPU v6e chip, on demand
Every correct answer has a price
The big model is accurate but expensive
It writes correct SQL for 60.7% of questions, and 1,000 correct answers cost $1.44.
The small model is cheap but often wrong
1,000 correct answers cost only $0.18, but it gets just 30.6% of questions right.
BIRD dev: 1,534 questions on 11 databases never used in training. Cost = $ per hour ÷ (requests per second × 3,600 × accuracy).
Let's start with the hardware. Our teacher, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, is a mixture-of-experts model with 552 billion parameters. One copy of it fills a whole server of eight H200 GPUs, which costs 36 dollars 60 an hour at the cheapest listed rate. GPUs like these are hard to get. Each copy of the model ties up a full server, so serving more users means renting more servers. A single TPU v6e chip costs 2 dollars 70 an hour. The question is whether we can move useful work from the left side of this slide to the right. We put a price on every correct answer. On the BIRD text-to-SQL benchmark, the teacher gets 60.7 percent of questions right, and a thousand correct answers cost a dollar 44. The untrained small model on one TPU chip costs 18 cents per thousand correct answers, but it gets less than a third of the questions right. We don't want either of these. We want a model in the top-left corner, one that is cheap and accurate. Keep this chart in mind, because we'll come back to it. ~3 min.
The problem

Generic small models miss domain details

QuestionWhich county is member Adela O'Gallagher's hometown in?
Untrained · SQLite syntax error
WHERE member.first_name = 'Adela'
  AND member.last_name = 'O\'Gallagher'
Trained student · correct rows
WHERE m.first_name = 'Adela'
  AND m.last_name = 'O''Gallagher'
Why fine-tune for the domain
The untrained 1.7B model gets only 10% of the hardest questions right. Of its wrong answers, 574 return the wrong rows and 462 are not valid SQLite, because the model invents columns or uses another dialect's syntax. Companies see the same problem with their own schemas and SQL dialects.
The bet
We bet that a big model could teach a small one, and that the small one could run on a single TPU chip.
Before we started, we set two targets: at least 5 points better than the untrained student, and at least 10× cheaper per correct answer than the teacher.
BIRD dev; accuracy by BIRD's difficulty label for the untrained Qwen3-1.7B; example dev-1347, question paraphrased
Here is what "weak in the domain" looks like, with a real BIRD question. The untrained small model escapes the apostrophe the way MySQL does, and SQLite rejects the query. After training, the student uses SQLite's doubled quote and gets the right rows. On the right you can see that the untrained model solves 40 percent of the simple questions and only 10 percent of the hardest ones. 462 of its wrong answers aren't even valid SQL. This is the gap companies care about: their own schemas and their own SQL dialect. Here was our bet. We use the big model as a teacher, train the small model on its answers, and serve the student on a single TPU chip. Before we started, we wrote down what success would mean: the student had to be at least five points better than before, with a confidence interval above zero, and at least ten times cheaper per correct answer than the teacher. We tested the bet three times, and the third test showed us where it breaks down. ~2.5 min.

Qwen3-1.7B starts weak
It is about 30 points behind the teacher on SQL and finance, so it has the most to learn. It is also the cheapest to serve.
Gemma 4 E2B starts strong

Teacher DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on 8× H200 for BIRD, FinQA and MATH; their students served by vLLM-TPU on one v6e chip; non-thinking mode throughout
Untrained student vs teacher, same prompt, greedy decoding; Qwen3-4B already scored 61.7% on BIRD and was not used
We ran four experiments with the same recipe. In BIRD, the model writes SQL against a database schema, and the grader runs the query and compares the rows. In FinQA, the model answers a numerical question about a page from an earnings report, which has text and a table, and the grader checks that the number is within one percent. In MATH, the model solves competition problems and puts its answer in a box, and the grader checks for an exact match. In the fourth, drawing, the model gets a short scene description, like "Green Tree On Grass Field", and writes an SVG document. Its automatic check is weaker: it confirms the output parses as SVG, but it can't say whether the picture matches the prompt, so we also compare the drawings ourselves. Each graded task is one module in the code, with its own prompt, answer extraction and grader. Everything else is shared: generation, verification, training and serving. Every grader also passes two checks: gold answers score 100 percent and shuffled answers score close to zero. We chose each student by how far it was behind the teacher, measured on the same benchmark with the same prompt. Qwen3-1.7B is about 30 points behind on both SQL and finance, so it has a lot to learn. The next size up, Qwen3-4B, already matched the teacher on BIRD, so there was nothing left to teach it. For the third experiment we picked a different kind of student on purpose: Gemma 4 E2B on competition maths. It is already strong, at 74.9 percent, and much closer to the teacher. That let us test whether a teacher still helps a student like that. For drawing, the student is Gemma 3 4B and the teacher is Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, a coding model less than twice its size. Untrained, Gemma 3 4B often ignores the prompt. ~4 min.
The experiments

Six decisions shaped the experiments

Tasks
Tasks with automatic graders
A program checks every answer, so one run takes minutes and can show a 2-point change. An agentic benchmark needs hours per run.
Students
A weak student and a strong one
With weak and strong students we can see when a teacher helps, and when it doesn't.
Training data
Only verified answers
The grader checks every training answer, because a wrong answer would teach the student the wrong thing.
Format
Short answers
Teacher and student both reason briefly. Without long reasoning traces, the teacher samples 4× faster.
Training
LoRA on one TPU host
LoRA fits on a single TPU v6e-8, and every size is a multiple of 256 to match the chip's matrix unit.
Evaluation
Comparisons within one run
We evaluate every model, a control and a second copy of the baseline together.
Six decisions shaped the experiments. We picked tasks with automatic graders, so a single run takes a few minutes and can show a two-point change. For drawing, the automatic check covers only the format, so we also look at the pictures. We used a weak student and a strong one, to see when a teacher helps. We trained only on verified answers. We kept answers short, without long reasoning traces. We trained with LoRA on one TPU host. And we compared models only within the same run, alongside a control and a second copy of the baseline. ~1.5 min.

Versions: vLLM 0.26.1rc1 TPU build, JAX 0.11.0, libtpu 0.0.44, Tunix 0.1.8, qwix 0.1.8, Flax 0.12.8, transformers 5.12.1 (docs/RECIPE.md)
Here is the whole process on one slide. All four experiments follow it. We measure the gap and the noise. We generate training answers, from the teacher for a weak student or from the student itself for a strong one. We check every answer with the task's grader. We distil with LoRA on one TPU host. We reinforce with GRPO. And we serve each student on one chip and work out the price of each answer. Distillation takes 10 to 27 minutes, and the final students are 4.8 to 17.5 times cheaper per correct answer than the teacher. Everything in the stack is open source. The teacher runs in Vertex AI Model Garden's vLLM container on eight H200s. The pipeline is plain Python standard-library scripts that write JSONL, so we can regenerate every number from the raw files. We serve students with vLLM-TPU, one copy per chip, and train them with Tunix and qwix LoRA in JAX on one v6e-8 host. The same trainer handles both Qwen3 and Gemma 4. The trainer, the server and storage all use one checkpoint format, Hugging Face safetensors. The drawing experiment runs as one Colab notebook: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B writes the SVGs, the student trains with QLoRA using transformers, peft and trl, and all three drawing models run on vLLM TPU inference. ~2.5 min.
The journey · steps 1–2 of 6

Measure the noise, then choose the training answers

1MeasureCheck the measurements before the experiment
What we didWe checked that every grader gives gold answers 100% and shuffled answers close to 0%. We also served two copies of each untrained model to measure noise.
DecisionWe compare models only within a single run, and every run includes a second copy of the baseline.
What we learnedGreedy decoding on vLLM-TPU isn't perfectly repeatable. Two copies of the same FinQA model differed by 1.9 points, so we can't trust a small gain without a noise floor.
2GenerateChoose who writes the training answers
What we didWe sampled the teacher 4 times and the student 8 times per question, using training questions only. Both write the same short format: brief reasoning, then one answer.
DecisionA weak student learns from the teacher's answers. A strong student learns from its own verified answers, which keep its style of reasoning.
What we learnedThe training answers should look like what the student will write when it serves. On MATH, the teacher's shorter solutions made a strong student worse.
* BIRD gold scores 100% of the 1,530 gold queries that execute (99.7% of 1,534)
Step one is to check the measurements before running the experiment. Every grader passes two checks: gold answers score 100 percent and shuffled answers score almost zero. Then we serve two copies of each untrained model side by side. On FinQA the two copies differ by 1.9 points, because greedy decoding on TPU serving isn't perfectly repeatable. So every comparison in this talk comes from a single run that includes a second copy of the baseline. The gaps to the teacher are 30, 32 and 18 points. Step two is choosing who writes the training answers. For a weak student, that's the teacher. We sample it four times per question at temperature 0.7, which gives 25 to 34 thousand answers per task in under 40 minutes. For a strong student, it's the student itself. We sample it eight times per question, and we don't need the teacher at all. We also train on the student's own answers as a control on every task, and on MATH that control won. Both teacher and student write the same short format: brief reasoning, then one answer. ~3 min.
The journey · steps 3–4 of 6

Verify every answer, then distil on one TPU host

3VerifyKeep only the answers the grader accepts
What we didWe graded every answer and kept only the correct ones, with up to four distinct answers per question. A separate audit re-checked every row and looked for overlap with the evaluation sets.
DecisionWe train only on verified answers, and we reject any row that comes from an evaluation database, report page or problem.
What we learnedThe grader turned out to be the most valuable code we wrote, because 40% of the teacher's BIRD answers were wrong. The audit found no leaks on any task.
4DistilDistil the student on one TPU host
What we didWe trained low-rank adapters on all eight chips of one TPU v6e-8 host, merged them into the model and exported a standard checkpoint for serving. Every task used the same settings.
DecisionWe used LoRA instead of full fine-tuning because it fits on one host. Every size is a multiple of 256 to match the TPU's matrix unit.
What we learnedBefore you trust a result, check that the trainer and the server compute the same model. Keep adapter weights in float32, because in bf16 the optimizer's first update divides zero by zero.
Step 3 bars: BIRD; table: FinQA and MATH (docs/RECIPE.md)
Step three is verification. Every answer goes through the task's grader, and we keep it only if it's correct. That threw out 40 percent of the teacher's BIRD answers and a quarter of its FinQA answers. The teacher is good, but it isn't perfect. On MATH we filter the student's own answers the same way. A separate audit re-grades every row we kept and checks for any overlap with the evaluation sets. It found no leaks on any of the three tasks. Step four is distillation. We train low-rank adapters on all eight chips of one TPU host, with the same settings on every task. That's 117, 69 and 57 optimizer steps, and 10 to 27 minutes of training. Before trusting any result, we checked that the training model and the serving model agree: they pick the same top token 99.8 percent of the time on Qwen3 and 99.4 percent on Gemma. A full retrain also reproduced a byte-identical checkpoint. One lesson we learned the hard way: adapter weights have to stay in float32. ~3 min.
The journey · steps 5–6 of 6

Reinforce with GRPO, then serve on a single chip

5ReinforceRL makes sometimes-right answers always right
What we didWe ran six rounds of GRPO. The student answers each training question 8 times, gets a reward of 1 when the grader accepts an answer, and moves toward the better answers in each group.
DecisionThe update learns only from questions with mixed outcomes, because all-right and all-wrong groups give it nothing to compare. A small KL penalty keeps the student close to where it started.
What we learnedOn FinQA, the share of questions the student always gets right grew from 43% to 61%, while the share it never gets right barely moved. On held-out data, RL added 4.0 points on BIRD, 5.8 on FinQA and 1.8 on MATH.
6ServeEach student runs on a single chip
What we didWe served every model with the same flags, one vLLM-TPU copy per chip, and raised the load until errors appeared. Then we priced the best error-free rate.
DecisionWe measure the cost of each correct answer, because both accuracy and throughput affect it. Tokens per second would ignore accuracy.
What we learnedAnswer length drives throughput. The trained BIRD student is faster than the untrained one, at 15.8 requests per second, but the MATH student's long answers make it slower than the teacher.
Step 5: training pool, 8 samples per question at T 1.0, policy that produced each round's samples; BIRD all-wrong = 100 − pass@8, all-right = pass@8 − mixed
Step 6: serving cost per 1,000 correct BIRD answers; student at the on-demand TPU v6e rate, teacher at the cheapest listed H200 rate
Step five is reinforcement learning. GRPO samples the student eight times per training question. An answer gets a reward of one if the grader accepts it, and the update pushes the student toward the better answers in each group. Only questions with mixed outcomes teach it anything. If all eight answers are right, or all eight are wrong, there's nothing to compare. The bars sort every training question, in every round, into three groups. Teal means all eight answers were right, gold means some were right, and gray means all eight were wrong. On FinQA the teal block grows from 43 to 61 percent, and it grows by taking over the gold block. The gray block barely changes. So RL takes answers the student can sometimes reach and makes it give them every time. It doesn't teach the student questions it never solves; that's what distillation is for. On held-out data, RL is worth 4 points on BIRD, 5.8 on FinQA and 1.8 on MATH. Step six is serving, and putting a price on each answer. Every model gets the same serving flags and one TPU chip per copy. We raise the load until the server starts returning errors, and we price the best rate it reached without errors. We measure cost per correct answer, because a fast wrong answer is worth nothing. On BIRD, a thousand correct answers from the trained student cost 9 cents. That's half the cost of the untrained model and a sixteenth of the teacher's. Answer length matters a lot here, as we'll see with MATH. ~3 min.
The journey · drawing

Drawing runs the same six steps

A coding model teaches. The teacher, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, is less than twice the size of the 4B student.
The check reads the format. It keeps SVGs that parse as XML with an <svg> root; it can't tell whether a drawing shows the prompt.
QLoRA on 20,000 drawings. One epoch, 1,250 steps in 2 h 31 min; training loss fell from 0.687 to 0.199.
The same serving stack. Teacher, untrained and distilled students all run on vLLM TPU inference.
Drawing run: one Colab notebook (transformers ≥ 4.50, peft ≥ 0.14, trl ≥ 0.14, bitsandbytes ≥ 0.45); the curve plots 1 − training loss
The drawing experiment uses the same six steps with a different pair of models. The teacher is Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, a coding model, and the student is Gemma 3 4B. We measure by rendering four test prompts for the teacher and the untrained student. The teacher writes 20,000 SVG drawings, about two valid ones per second, and we keep only the ones that parse as SVG. Then we distil with QLoRA: one epoch, 1,250 steps, two and a half hours, and the training loss falls from 0.69 to 0.20. We didn't run RL on drawing. All three models serve on vLLM TPU inference. The difference from the other tasks is the check: it tells us a drawing is valid SVG, not that it shows the right thing. So for drawing we look at the pictures, which is where the results start. ~1.5 min.

Each panel: one same-run evaluation; KD = teacher answers, Self = the student's own verified answers; dashed line = teacher; paired differences with bootstrap 95% CIs
BIRD dev, 1,534 questions; FinQA test, 1,147 questions, settings and schedule unchanged from BIRD; MATH test, 5,000 problems
Every graded task improved, and every confidence interval is above zero. On BIRD, accuracy went from 30.6 to 52.2 percent, a gain of 21.6 points. On FinQA it went from 44 to 72.5 percent, a gain of 28.4 points, which is only three points short of the teacher. On MATH, Gemma went from 74.9 to 78.4 percent, a gain of 3.5 points. Look at the middle bar for MATH: it isn't trained on the teacher's data. On MATH, the best recipe trained the student on its own answers. The numbers under each chart split every gain into its steps. Let's look at BIRD. On 1,534 questions over eleven databases the student never saw, accuracy went from 30.6 to 48.2 percent after distillation, and to 52.2 after GRPO. The teacher scores 60.7. Distillation gave the biggest gain, 17.6 points, and RL added four more. The final student closed 72 percent of the gap to the teacher, and producing it cost 136 dollars of compute. FinQA was our replication. We used the same student, the same teacher, the same settings and the same six-round schedule, all fixed before the run. The only new code was the task module. On 1,147 test questions, accuracy went from 44 to 66.6 percent after distillation and to 72.5 after GRPO, 3.2 points short of the teacher. Both gains are far larger than the noise, and the final student closed 90 percent of the gap for 79 dollars. ~3 min.

What we got

The control experiment tells us which recipe to use

What the control is. We train the same SFT recipe on the same number of rows, using the student's own verified answers instead of the teacher's.
The weak student learns more from the teacher. The teacher's answers beat the student's own by 13.1 points on BIRD and 9.6 on FinQA.
The strong student learns more from itself. On MATH, the teacher's answers score 4.3 points lower than the student's own.
A strong student lost accuracy copying the teacher
597 vs 1,027
average tokens per answer. The distilled student copied the teacher's shorter solutions.
−3.3 / −4.1
points lost on the two hardest levels, where short solutions hurt most
−10.8
points when the teacher corrected the student's mistakes instead
Lesson
Gemma already reasons well in its own style. Copying the teacher's shorter style cost it accuracy, while training on its own answers improved it.
Left: teacher-answer SFT minus self-distillation SFT, paired differences in points with bootstrap 95% CIs, same-run evaluations
Right: MATH test, 5,000 problems, same-run evaluation; teacher corrections from a separate same-run evaluation
If you remember one slide from this talk, make it this one. In every experiment we trained a control: the same recipe on the same number of rows, but with the student's own verified answers instead of the teacher's. The chart shows the teacher's result minus the control's. For the weak student, the teacher's answers clearly win, by 13 points on BIRD and 10 on FinQA. For the strong student it goes the other way: the teacher's answers score 4.3 points lower than the student's own. One extra SFT run told us which recipe each student needed. Why did the teacher's answers hurt on MATH? Gemma already reasons well, and it writes long solutions. The teacher writes much shorter ones, about 600 tokens compared with Gemma's thousand. The distilled student copied that style and lost the most on the two hardest levels. It isn't running out of room, either: it hits the length limit less often than before. We also tried teacher corrections, where the teacher sees the student's failed answer and writes a fix, and we train on the fixes. That was even worse, at minus 10.8 points. Training on the student's own verified answers gained about two points. ~3 min.
What we got

Counting cut-off answers as wrong made RL work

Problems per roundwith mixed outcomes
Lesson
About 15% of the student's MATH answers hit the 2,048-token limit before giving an answer, and our original GRPO threw them away. Once we scored them as wrong, the update had twice as many problems to learn from, and GRPO added 1.82 points [+1.00, +2.66] instead of 0.84.
MATH test, 5,000 problems, same-run evaluation; 6 GRPO rounds each; cut-off answers keep reward 0 and no end-of-turn token in the loss
We had to make one more change before RL worked for the strong student. Gemma's most common failure is running out of room: about 15 percent of its answers hit the 2,048-token limit before giving a final answer. Our original GRPO threw those answers away, so the student's main failure never got a negative reward. We kept them, gave them a reward of zero, and trained only on the tokens the student actually wrote. That doubled the number of problems with mixed outcomes in each round, from about 600 to 1,300, and GRPO then added 1.82 points instead of 0.84. ~1.5 min.

Why we trust these results
Repeat runs agree. Three BIRD evaluations gave +17.8, +18.1 and +17.6. Four MATH evaluations stayed between +1.3 and +1.9.
No evaluation data leaked. A row-by-row audit found no evaluation database, report page or problem in the training data.
The results reproduce. A retrain produced a byte-identical model, and one script regenerates every number.
Chart: BIRD. Teacher at its cheapest listed H200 rate, students at the on-demand TPU rate; cost ratio = 13.6 × throughput × accuracy
Right: paired differences in points with bootstrap 95% CIs; each row from a same-run evaluation
Here's the chart from the start of the talk again. On BIRD, the trained student landed where we wanted it, in the cheap and accurate corner. It's 15.8 times cheaper per correct answer than the teacher. The table covers all three tasks. Hardware price gives a factor of 13.6 everywhere, and throughput and accuracy decide the rest. FinQA reaches 17.5 times. MATH reaches only 4.8 times, because Gemma's long answers make one chip slower than the teacher's eight GPUs. Short answers save real money. Drawing has no cost figure, because we didn't measure its serving throughput. Why should you believe these numbers? Every gain sits next to its own noise floor, which we measured in the same run with two copies of the untrained model. The SQL and finance gains are about ten times the noise. The MATH gain is small, 3.5 points, but its interval is well clear of the noise. Repeat evaluations agree within a point, the audit found no leaks, a retrain was byte-identical, and one script regenerates every number. ~3 min.
Similar approaches

Meta's TorchTitan RL work found similar lessons

TorchTitan RL · MetaTPU-Distil
Tasklong-horizon terminal agents; Terminal-Bench, 89 hard taskssingle-turn SQL, finance, maths and SVG drawing answers
StudentQwen3.5-9BQwen3-1.7B, Gemma 4 E2B, Gemma 3 4B
Hardware8× B300: 2 trainer, 5 rollout, 1 eval workers1 TPU v6e-8 host; teacher on 8× H200
Starting pointRL on ~1,000 cleaned tasksdistil verified answers, then RL
AlgorithmDPPO, loss averaged per promptGRPO, PPO clip, KL to the start
Samplingasynchronous, never pauses; weights hot-swappedsynchronous rounds: sample, then update
Result+52% on Terminal-Bench after 33 h of RL+21.6 / +28.4 / +3.5 points; $79–$159
Both cleaned the data
Only 42% of Meta's tasks were clean before repair, and 40% of our teacher's BIRD answers were wrong.
Both checked the numerics
A compiled kernel gave Meta a 2.5× log-prob mismatch. We check that our trainer and server agree.
Both reward failures
Meta penalises a missing submission, and we score cut-off answers as wrong.
Meta figures from the speaker's notes of "Training long-horizon agents with TorchTitan RL", PyTorch Conference 2026; TPU-Distil figures from the README
How does this compare with other work? At the PyTorch Conference, Meta presented TorchTitan RL for long-horizon agents. They trained a Qwen3.5 9B model with RL on about a thousand cleaned terminal tasks, using eight B300s split into trainer, rollout and eval workers that run fully asynchronously. Their problem and scale are different. They go straight to RL on multi-turn agents, while we distil first and then run RL on single-turn answers. But the lessons are similar. Both projects cleaned the data first: only 42 percent of their tasks were clean, and 40 percent of our teacher's answers were wrong. Both checked the numerics: a compiled kernel gave them a 2.5x log-prob mismatch, and we check that our trainer and server agree. And both had to reward failures carefully. They treat a dead sandbox, a missing submission and the context limit differently, and our MATH fix, counting cut-off answers as wrong, is the same idea. ~2 min.
Takeaways

What we learned

+22 / +28 / +3.5
points gained on SQL, finance and maths by students of about 2B parameters
4.8–17.5×
cheaper per correct answer than the 552B teacher
$79–$159
of compute to produce each student on one TPU host
If the student is weak, distil the teacher. The teacher's verified answers gave most of the gain.
If the student is strong, let it learn from itself. Its own verified answers beat the teacher's.
Then add RL. Make sure the student's main failure gets a negative reward.
Measure carefully. Compare models in one run, with a control and a noise floor, price each correct answer, and look at the outputs when the check reads only the format.
How to run this recipe on your own taskgithub.com/jawadaminGOOG/tpu-distil
1Measure
Score the teacher and a few candidate students with one prompt, and measure the noise floor.
grade.py · gold + shuffled controls
2Generate
Sample the teacher 4 times and the student 8 times per question, at temperature 0.7.
generate.py
3Verify
Keep the answers your grader accepts, up to 4 distinct per question, and audit for leaks.
build_sft.py · leak_audit.py
4Distil
Train LoRA on both data sets (rank 256, lr 1e-4, batch 256, 3 epochs) and keep the better one.
train_tpu_vm.sh sft
5Reinforce
Run GRPO with 8 samples at temperature 1.0, and count cut-off answers as wrong.
build_grpo_rollouts.py --keep-truncated
6Serve and price
Serve on vLLM-TPU with one copy per chip, then work out the cost per correct answer.
serve_small.sh · bench_serving.py
How to choose the recipe. Train on the teacher's answers and on the student's own answers side by side. If the teacher's answers win, use KD + GRPO. If the student's own answers win, use self-distillation + GRPO, which needs no teacher time.
Code, settings and commands: github.com/jawadaminGOOG/tpu-distil (README recipe, docs/RECIPE.md)
To wrap up: we used one recipe on four tasks with three students. A 1.7-billion-parameter student gained 22 points on SQL and 28 on finance, a strong Gemma student gained 3.5 points on competition maths, and a 4-billion-parameter Gemma learned to draw like its 7-billion-parameter coding teacher. The graded students are 4.8 to 17.5 times cheaper per correct answer than the 552-billion-parameter teacher, and each one cost 79 to 159 dollars of compute to produce. If your student is weak, distil the teacher. If it's strong, let it learn from its own answers. Then add RL, and make sure the student's main failure gets a negative reward. And measure carefully, and when the check can only read the format, look at the outputs. Here's the recipe, so you can try it on your own task. Measure the gap and the noise with one prompt. Generate two training sets, one from the teacher and one from the student itself. Keep only the answers your grader accepts, and check for leaks. Distil both sets with the same LoRA settings and keep the better one. That one comparison tells you whether your student is weak or strong. Then run GRPO with the grader as the reward, and count cut-off answers as wrong. Finally, serve on single chips and work out the price of a correct answer. The code you write is one task module. It loads the questions, builds a versioned prompt, extracts the answer and grades it, with gold and shuffled checks. We added FinQA and MATH exactly this way. Thank you; we're happy to take questions. ~3 min.

A8Appendix
Supports slide 8 · Six decisions shaped the experiments

We fixed the evaluation design before seeing results

Targets set in advance
We wrote down the pass conditions before each stage.
Test sets stayed untouched
No evaluation set chose a checkpoint or a hyperparameter, and we fixed the final checkpoint in advance.
One run per comparison
We serve and grade every compared model together, with greedy decoding and a 2,048-token limit.
Two copies of the baseline
Every run includes two copies of the untrained model, which give the noise floor.
Paired statistics
We compare models question by question and report bootstrap 95% CIs from 10,000 resamples.
Early stopping
BIRD used only its 522 held-out training-database questions for early stopping.
docs/RECIPE.md §7, README limits
Backup for slide 8 (Six decisions shaped the experiments). This is how we avoided tuning on the test set.
A9Appendix
Supports slide 8 · Six decisions shaped the experiments

Answer length is a serving cost

Why we turned thinking off
Teacher and student both answer briefly. The student would copy long reasoning traces, and the teacher samples 4× faster without them.
Lesson
On MATH the student's answers are 2.3× longer than the teacher's, so one chip finishes fewer requests than eight GPUs, and throughput drops to 0.42×.
Bars: teacher ÷ student cost per correct answer (README)

What it took to add Gemma 4

ProblemFix
vLLM-TPU warm-up fails on the default PyTorch model pathMODEL_IMPL_TYPE=flax_nnx: the JAX Gemma 4 model

Tunix's Gemma 4 model handles per-layer embeddings and KV sharing. LoRA covers the fused k/v in the 15 layers that compute K/V, and the logit soft-cap runs in float32.

A28Appendix
Supports slide 19 · Counting cut-off answers as wrong made RL work

How we score cut-off answers

build_grpo_rollouts.py --keep-truncated
rollout hits 2,048 tokens
  no end-of-turn token emitted

before: dropped from its group
  -> the main failure never gets
     a negative reward

now:    kept, reward 0,
        "truncated": true
  -> data.py gives the trailing
     end-of-turn token weight 0
~600 → ~1,300
MATH problems per round with mixed outcomes
+0.98
scored wrong vs dropped, CI [+0.16, +1.78]
Why we drop the end-of-turn token
If we trained on a cut-off answer as written, the student would learn to stop where it never stopped. Leaving out the end-of-turn token lowers the probability of exactly the tokens it wrote.

A31Appendix
Supports slide 20 · Why we trust these results

What these results don't show

One training seed
We trained each model once, so the noise floor measures serving noise, not training-seed variance.
Student and task changed together
The student changed along with the task, so "already strong" is our best explanation, not a proven cause.
Public benchmarks
The teacher and students may have seen BIRD, FinQA or MATH during pre-training. This applies to every model.
The FinQA grader is lenient
It accepts a 1% tolerance and percentage forms, so our scores aren't comparable to published FinQA results.
We missed the MATH targets
We required KD to gain 5 points (it lost 2.3) and each GRPO stage to gain 2 (the best gained 1.82). A 7-hour outage cut one round to 3,367 of 6,262 problems.
The cost gap depends on deployment
A faster teacher deployment would shrink the cost advantage (see A2).
README, what this does not show
Backup for slide 20 (Why we trust these results). These are the caveats we state up front.

No serving cost
We didn't measure drawing throughput, so there is no cost per correct drawing.
No RL
We didn't run GRPO on drawing.
A different trainer
The drawing student trained with QLoRA in a Colab notebook, not with the Tunix TPU trainer.
One training run
We trained the drawing student once, like the other students.

Adding your own task or student

A new task is one module
# distil/tasks/<your_task>.py
load_items(split)      -> items
PROMPT_VERSION, render(item)
extract(response)      -> answer
grade(answer, item)    -> bool

# controls before use
gold answers   ~ 100%
shuffled       ~ 0%

# then: add the name to NAMES
Adding a new student
Add a config builder, loader, LoRA targets and delta exporter in student_models.py, and its end-of-turn marker in data.py.
Before you train
Check logit parity with parity_check.py, and check the served chat template with vLLM's /tokenize. We added FinQA, MATH and Gemma 4 this way.

A36Appendix
Supports slide 21 · Meta's TorchTitan RL work found similar lessons

A closer look at TorchTitan RL

Sampling never pauses
Rollouts run continuously, new weights are swapped in while they run, and the buffer takes any 32 finished groups in any order.
The KV cache survives updates
They keep it across weight updates with no accuracy loss. KV headroom limits how many rollouts run in parallel.
The agent runs outside the sandbox
The policy controls a sandbox but doesn't run inside it.
Each failure gets its own reward
A dead sandbox gets no penalty, a missing submission gets a penalty, and hitting the context limit gets a nudge.
They cleaned the tasks
Only 42% of TMAX tasks and 61% of CalibForge tasks were clean before repair.
DPPO with per-prompt averaging
They use DPPO instead of GRPO or PPO, and average the loss per prompt instead of per token.
Speaker's notes of "Training long-horizon agents with TorchTitan RL", PyTorch Conference 2026
Backup for slide 21 (Meta's TorchTitan RL work found similar lessons). These are the design choices Meta described for TorchTitan RL on Terminal-Bench.

Supports slide 21 · Meta's TorchTitan RL work found similar lessons

What we'd borrow from TorchTitan RL

Idea from TorchTitan RLWhere it fits in TPU-DistilWhy
Asynchronous rolloutsoverlap sampling and updates across the 8 chipsrollouts were 30% of BIRD and 58% of MATH chip-hours, with the trainer idle
Online task generation (+8 points vs a static pool)generate new questions per round from training datalater FinQA rounds ran out of mixed-outcome questions
Failure-type rewardsextend the MATH cut-off rule to other failure typeseach failure mode needs its own signal
Bitwise trainer–sampler paritytighten parity from 0.998 top-1 toward exactremoves a source of off-policy drift
Per-prompt loss averagingan option in the GRPO losslong answers stop dominating the update
These are ideas; we haven't tested any of them in TPU-Distil
